31.layer4_ar: يتفق علماء الشيعة والسنة على أن هذه الآية تُثبت سيادة مشيئة الله مع تأكيد المسؤولية الأخلاقية الإنسانية. ويُبيِّن فخر الدين الرازي في مفاتيح الغيب أن مشيئة الله في إدخال الناس رحمته تقوم على علمه الأزلي بخياراتهم مما يصون سعة العلم الإلهي ويحترم الفاعلية الإنسانية. ويُشدِّد القرطبي في الجامع لأحكام القرآن على أن الظلم يُخرج أصحابه من الرحمة لا لأن الله قليل الرحمة بل لأنهم بإصرارهم على رفض الهداية جعلوا أنفسهم غير قابلين للرحمة. والفارق الرئيسي في التفسير يتمحور حول طبيعة المشيئة الإلهية والقدرة الإنسانية؛ إذ يُشدِّد العلم الشيعي المستمَدُّ من تعاليم أهل البيت على أن الإنسان يتمتع بإرادة حرة حقيقية وأن مشيئة الله تعمل بمنح الناس نتائج اختياراتهم مما يجعل العدل الإلهي مُدرَكاً والمحاسبة الأخلاقية ذات معنى. وتميل بعض التيارات السنية إلى تأكيد القدر أكثر وإن كانت المذاهب السنية الكبرى كالأشاعرة والماتريدية تُثبت هي أيضاً المسؤولية الإنسانية. ويتفق الفريقان على أن رحمة الله واسعةٌ في متناول الجميع عبر التوبة الصادقة وأن العذاب الأليم مُعَدٌّ للمُصرِّين على الظلم حتى الموت. وتُفهم الآية في الدراسة العلمية الإسلامية على اختلاف مذاهبها تذكيراً أخيراً في سورة الإنسان بأن رحمة الله والجنة معروضتان بسخاء لكنها تستلزم استقبالاً إنسانياً بالإيمان والعمل الصالح.
31.layer1: This final verse of Surah Al-Insan brings the surah to a powerful and sobering close. Allah declares that He admits into His mercy whomever He wills, while the wrongdoers — those who reject His guidance, deny His messengers, and persist in disobedience — will face a grievous and painful punishment. The verse serves as a seal on the entire surah, which opened with a reflection on the origins of the human being and moved through the qualities of the righteous, the rewards of Paradise, and the challenge of following the straight path. The key Arabic term here is 'al-zalimeen,' meaning the wrongdoers or oppressors, which in this context refers primarily to those who wrong their own souls by rejecting the truth. The phrase 'yudkhilu man yasha fi rahmatih' — He admits into His mercy whom He wills — affirms that divine mercy is a gift, not an entitlement, and that it is distributed according to Allah's infinite wisdom and knowledge. This verse is both a message of hope for believers who seek Allah's mercy and a warning for those who choose heedlessness. Practically, this verse encourages Muslims to never despair of Allah's mercy while simultaneously remaining vigilant against the path of wrongdoing. The verse also teaches the importance of humility before Allah, recognising that entry into His mercy is ultimately by His grace and not solely by human effort.
31.layer2: Imam al-Tabari in his Jami al-Bayan explains that this verse establishes the absolute sovereignty of Allah in dispensing mercy and punishment. He notes that the construction of the verse — positioning 'al-zalimeen' at the front of the second clause before its governing verb — is a rhetorical device of emphasis (takhsis), singling out the wrongdoers for special attention and stressing that their punishment has been definitively prepared. Al-Tabari connects this to the broader theological principle that guidance is in Allah's hands alone, and no human can compel divine mercy upon themselves. Ibn Kathir in Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim takes a similar approach, linking this verse directly to the preceding verse (76:30) which established that human volition itself operates within the framework of divine will. Ibn Kathir explains that 'He admits whom He wills into His mercy' means Allah guides whom He wills to Islam and righteous deeds, and these are the ones who receive the eternal rewards described earlier in the surah. The wrongdoers are those who, despite the revelation reaching them, deliberately and persistently choose to reject it. Ibn Kathir draws support from the companion tradition (athar al-sahabah) to indicate that 'al-zalimeen' encompasses all categories of oppressors, with the greatest oppression being shirk and kufr. Al-Qurtubi in his Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran adds a fiqhi dimension, noting this verse demonstrates that salvation is not earned purely through works but is ultimately a bestowal of divine mercy, consistent with the well-known hadith in Sahih Bukhari in which the Prophet, peace be upon him, said that no one will enter Paradise by their deeds alone, and when asked about himself, he confirmed this applies to him too unless Allah envelops him in His mercy.
31.layer3: Contemporary scholars find in this concluding verse a rich convergence of theology, human psychology, and social accountability. Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran reflects that the surah closes on a note of divine majesty — the same majesty with which it opened when it reminded humanity of its lowly origins. He observes that the final verse dissolves any sense of human arrogance: after all the descriptions of Paradise, the beautiful rewards, the noble qualities of the righteous, the conclusion is that entry into mercy is by Allah's will, not a right that anyone can claim. This, Qutb argues, keeps the believer in a state of perpetual aspiration, gratitude, and servitude. Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir emphasises the grammatical fronting of 'al-zalimeen' as an intensification technique, arguing it reflects the Quran's consistent pattern of balancing mercy and warning to keep the human soul in balance between hope (raja) and fear (khawf). Ibn Uthaymeen, in his explanations of Quranic theology, frequently highlighted that such verses refute two extreme positions: the Mutazilite view that humans earn Paradise purely by their efforts, and a fatalistic quietism that abandons personal responsibility. The Sunni position, as crystallised in this verse, is that human choice is real and consequential, but mercy remains Allah's gift. In the modern context, this verse speaks powerfully to the culture of entitlement and self-sufficiency; it reminds contemporary believers that no amount of material achievement, intellectual status, or social standing substitutes for sincere reliance on Allah's grace and active avoidance of oppression and wrongdoing in all its forms.
